\textbf{What it costs.} First, forecasts are compressed toward the middle. Merit sensitivity with own accounts falls from <<ms0:G:base.PA.fmean>> to <<ms0:G:g2.PA.fmean>> points, and with agreed facts, where there is nothing to discount, from <<ms0:G:base.N.fmean>> to <<ms0:G:g2.N.fmean>>. Second Chair is not the ``split it'' advisor that the control is there to expose, but it has moved part of the way. Second, it is not measurably more accurate. The distance between the forecast a party is given and the neutral helper's forecast from the full agreed facts is <<e:G:g2.PA.err>> points against <<e:G:base.PA.err>> in the base arm (difference <<e:G:g2-base.PA.err>>, interval <<lo:G:g2-base.PA.err>> to <<hi:G:g2-base.PA.err>>), on a scale where two independent neutral replies already differ by <<e:obs.noise>>; on agreed facts it is slightly larger (<<e:G:g2.N.err>> against <<e:G:base.N.err>>). The two sides now hear compatible forecasts; neither hears one much closer to what the model would say with both stories. Third, it recommends talking or mediation in <<x:Gstep23:g2|PA>>\% of conversations, whatever the merits; whether that is right for a strong claim that the other side has already refused is a question for mediators.

G1_TEXT: \textbf{The cheap alternative overshoots.} The one-paragraph prompt (g1) also removes most of the impasse (rate <<e0:G:g1.PA.impasse>>\%, interval <<lo0:G:g1.PA.impasse>> to <<hi0:G:g1.PA.impasse>>) with a single call, keeps merit sensitivity with own accounts (<<ms0:G:g1.PA.fmean>> points) and is slightly closer there to the full-information forecast (<<e:G:g1.PA.err>> against <<e:G:base.PA.err>>). But it reverses the bias instead of removing it. Each party is now told an outcome that is \emph{worse} for itself than the other party is told: the role gap is <<ci:G:g1.PA.rg>> points with own accounts and <<ci:G:g1.N.rg>> on agreed facts, where the base arm had no gap at all. Asked in one breath to consider the other side and to say where the user is weak, the models talk their own user down. Second Chair's assessor, which does not know whom it is writing for, leaves role gaps of <<ci:G:g2.N.rg>> and <<ci:G:g2.PA.rg>>.

DISCUSSION_PRODUCT: For builders of ``angel'' assistants, the default advisor is a faithful amplifier of whatever account it is given, and one added step (an assessment that must allow for the unheard side) makes two parties' advice compatible. Its cost in sharpness is something a product can expose, for example by showing the forecast with and without the discount, or by asking for the other party's likely version before forecasting at all.
CONCLUSION: When each side of a dispute brings its own story to the same chatbot, the advice they receive is mutually incompatible in <<e0:base.P.impasse>>\% of cases, and in <<e0:base.PA.impasse>>\% if they are angry. The cause is less flattery than credulity: on agreed facts the models forecast the same outcome for both sides, and a neutral reader of a one-sided account is misled nearly as much as the party's own advisor. A second opinion that must allow for the unheard side removes most of the incompatibility, and its weakness, forecasts pulled toward the middle, is measurable with the same two-sided instrument.
